sources.author: Mauricio Karchmer, Ilan Newman, Mike Saks & Avi Wigderson
sources.locator: Sections 2.1-2.3, printed pp. 3-5; Proposition 3 and proof

nodes.label: Weighted graph
nodes.summary: Objects joined by connections, each carrying a numerical weight.
nodes.explanation: Here weights are positive conductances. A graph records which vertices are joined and the weight of each connection; using it to model an application requires additional assumptions.

nodes.label: Graph Laplacian
nodes.summary: A matrix that measures differences between neighbouring vertices.
nodes.explanation: Place each weighted degree on the diagonal and negative edge weights off the diagonal. Multiplying by a vector compares each value with its neighbours.

nodes.label: Dirichlet energy
nodes.summary: A score for how much values change across graph edges.
nodes.explanation: A large difference across a highly conducting edge contributes more energy. This quadratic form connects the graph to electrical dissipation.

evidence.locator: Section 14.2 (energy of a flow and electrical dissipation)

nodes.label: Electrical flow
nodes.summary: Currents move through a resistive network under imposed injections.
nodes.explanation: Voltage differences and conductances determine currents. One unit enters at one vertex and leaves at another.

nodes.label: Effective resistance
nodes.summary: The voltage needed to send one unit of current between two vertices.
nodes.explanation: Multiple routes can lower the effective resistance. Its role reaches beyond circuits into the probabilities of graph edges appearing in spanning trees.

nodes.label: Spanning tree
nodes.summary: A connected selection of edges that reaches every vertex without a cycle.
nodes.explanation: A connected finite graph can have many spanning trees. Weighting each tree by the product of its edge weights defines a probability distribution.

nodes.label: Edge inclusion probability
nodes.summary: How often an edge appears in a random spanning tree.
nodes.explanation: For a tree drawn with probability proportional to its edge-weight product, an edge's inclusion probability is its conductance times its effective resistance.

nodes.label: Edge leverage score
nodes.summary: A numerical measure of an edge's role in the network.
nodes.explanation: For these graph edges the leverage score is conductance times effective resistance. A bridge that is the only connection between two parts has score one.

nodes.label: Degree matrix
nodes.summary: A diagonal matrix of weighted vertex degrees.
nodes.explanation: Each entry is the sum of the conductances incident to that vertex. Together with adjacency, it defines the Laplacian.

nodes.label: Adjacency matrix
nodes.summary: A matrix recording which vertices are connected.
nodes.explanation: An off-diagonal entry gives the edge weight. In this undirected setting the matrix is symmetric.

nodes.label: Conductance
nodes.summary: How readily an edge carries current.
nodes.explanation: Conductance is the reciprocal of resistance. The atlas's computational lab initially uses conductance one on every edge.

nodes.label: Ohm’s law
nodes.summary: Current through a resistor is proportional to its voltage drop.
nodes.explanation: For an ohmic edge, conductance times voltage difference gives current. This physical assumption defines the circuit model here.

nodes.label: Harmonic function on a graph
nodes.summary: At an interior vertex, the value equals its weighted neighbour average.
nodes.explanation: The Laplacian is zero there. Fixed boundary values determine the interior when every relevant component reaches the boundary.
assumptions: Finite undirected graph with positive conductances
Each interior component connects to a fixed boundary

nodes.label: Dirichlet boundary problem
nodes.summary: Find interior values from specified boundary values.
nodes.explanation: Solve a reduced linear system. The solution also minimizes the quadratic energy subject to those same boundary values.
assumptions: Nonempty boundary meeting each connected component

nodes.label: Random walk on a graph
nodes.summary: A process that repeatedly moves to a neighbouring vertex.
nodes.explanation: In the unweighted model each neighbour is equally likely. Long-run travel behaviour can be studied using the same network as an electrical circuit.

nodes.label: Expected hitting time
nodes.summary: The expected steps needed to reach a specified target.
nodes.explanation: First-step equations express the value as one step plus the average of the neighbours' values. Travel in opposite directions need not have equal expectation.
assumptions: Target is absorbing for the hitting-time calculation

nodes.label: Commute time
nodes.summary: Expected steps to travel from one vertex to another and back.
nodes.explanation: It is the sum of the two directed hitting times. The resistance identity applies to this sum, not to either direction individually.

nodes.label: Commute–resistance identity
nodes.summary: Electrical resistance determines random-walk round-trip time.
nodes.explanation: Replace each graph edge with a unit resistor. Twice the edge count times the effective resistance gives the commute time.

nodes.label: First-hit probability
nodes.summary: The chance of reaching one labelled boundary before another.
nodes.explanation: Unlike expected hitting time, this quantity measures a probability. In a seeded image model it supplies a label score.

nodes.label: Matrix–Tree theorem
nodes.summary: Laplacian eigenvalues encode the total weight of spanning trees.
nodes.explanation: For a connected weighted graph, the product of the nonzero Laplacian eigenvalues is n times the sum of the tree-weight products.
nodes.formula: Πᵢ₌₂ⁿ λᵢ = n Σᵀ Πₑ∈ᵀ wₑ

nodes.label: Resistance distance
nodes.summary: Effective resistance is also a distance on graph vertices.
nodes.explanation: It satisfies the triangle inequality. A squared-Euclidean representation exists, which must not be confused with claiming resistance itself is a Euclidean norm.

nodes.label: Schur complement
nodes.summary: Eliminate interior variables while retaining boundary behaviour.
nodes.explanation: For a network Laplacian, the reduced matrix sends retained boundary voltages to their external currents after the interior has equilibrated.
assumptions: Interior vertices have no external current

nodes.label: Vertex elimination
nodes.summary: Replace interior network vertices by an equivalent boundary network.
nodes.explanation: The replacement preserves the stated boundary current–voltage map. It does not preserve every internal path or every interior query.

nodes.label: Series and parallel rules
nodes.summary: Simple arrangements allow direct resistance calculations.
nodes.explanation: Resistances add along a series path; conductances add for parallel connections. General graphs require additional methods.
assumptions: Resistors in the specified series or parallel configuration

nodes.label: Resistance-based sampling
nodes.summary: Sample edges according to their conductance times resistance.
nodes.explanation: The sparsification algorithm samples with replacement and reweights the sampled edges. Its guarantee depends on sample count and error parameters.
assumptions: Specified sampling count and approximation parameter

nodes.label: Spectral approximation
nodes.summary: Two graphs have similar energy for every vector of vertex values.
nodes.explanation: The comparison is multiplicative and includes an error parameter. It does not require the graphs to have the same edges.

nodes.label: Spectral sparsifier
nodes.summary: A weighted subgraph that approximately preserves every Laplacian quadratic form.
nodes.explanation: The aim is to retain the energy of every vector while using a sparse set of reweighted edges. This is useful when the input is dense; strict edge reduction is not guaranteed for every input. The resistance-sampling construction has separate size, accuracy and probability conditions in the source theorem.
nodes.formula: (1 - epsilon) x^T L_G x <= x^T L_H x <= (1 + epsilon) x^T L_G x for all x
assumptions: The graphs have the same vertex set
Positive edge weights; approximation is for every vector
For the cited construction, Theorem 1 imposes sufficiently large n, 1/sqrt(n) < epsilon <= 1, its specified sample count q and a probability of success at least 1/2
A sparse-edge bound does not imply fewer edges than every possible input graph

nodes.label: Pixel graph
nodes.summary: An image represented by vertices and weighted neighbour connections.
nodes.explanation: A modelling choice turns local image relationships into graph weights. Seed labels provide boundary information for the random-walker method.

nodes.label: Seeded image segmentation
nodes.summary: Assign image regions using labelled seeds and random-walk probabilities.
nodes.explanation: Each unlabelled pixel receives the label with the largest first-hit probability. The model does not remove the need to choose seeds and weights.
nodes.formula: label(u) = argmaxₖ Pr(first seed has label k)
assumptions: Every unlabelled component reaches a seed

nodes.label: Chemical graph invariants
nodes.summary: Graph quantities used to describe structure in chemical graph theory.
nodes.explanation: Resistance-based sums provide mathematical descriptors. A descriptor alone establishes no empirical relationship to a material property.

nodes.label: Resistance-distance sums
nodes.summary: Combine vertex-pair resistance distances into graph invariants.
nodes.explanation: Klein studies global and local sum rules and relationships between invariants. These connect electrical-network mathematics to chemical graph theory.

nodes.label: Kemeny's constant
nodes.summary: An average of random-walk travel times to destinations weighted by their long-run fraction of visits.
nodes.explanation: At each step choose a neighbouring vertex uniformly. Choose a destination with probability proportional to its degree. With zero steps assigned when the destination is the starting point, the expected number of steps to reach that destination is Kemeny's constant. It has the same value for every starting vertex.
nodes.formula: K(G) = sum_j (d_j / (2m)) H_ij = d^T R d / (4m)
assumptions: Finite connected simple undirected unweighted graph with at least two vertices
Simple random walk P = D^-1 A
Destination probabilities are recomputed when graph degrees change

evidence.locator: Section 2.1, hitting-time definition and Theorem 2.1; Section 2.2, graph transition matrix and resistance formula

nodes.label: Braess set for a random walk
nodes.summary: A group of added connections that increases Kemeny's constant.
nodes.explanation: Under the strict convention used here, a missing edge or set of missing edges is Braess when adding it makes K larger. The effect of adding edges together can differ from their individual effects. This compares a specific random-walk statistic; it does not by itself establish slower traffic, a longer shortest path, or worse performance for an application.
assumptions: The same connected simple undirected unweighted graph model and K convention
S is a nonempty set of distinct missing edges
Strict increase; exact equality is not classified as Braess here

evidence.locator: Definition 4.1 and the P7 example immediately after Corollary 4.3

nodes.label: Boolean relation matrix
nodes.summary: A finite yes-or-no table representing which labeled row and column choices are related.
nodes.explanation: Choose finite nonempty labeled sets X and Y. The entry A[x,y] is 1 exactly when x is related to y. For a Boolean function f, its communication matrix is M_f[x,y]=f(x,y). The all-zero table keeps the same nonempty row and column sets.
assumptions: X and Y are finite, nonempty and labeled
A rectangular X-by-Y matrix is not automatically the full symmetric adjacency matrix of a graph

evidence.locator: Introduction, printed p. 2, Boolean-matrix and bipartite-adjacency paragraphs

nodes.label: Boolean rank
nodes.summary: The fewest Boolean rank-one factors whose OR-AND product reconstructs a binary matrix.
nodes.explanation: A factor index chooses one set of rows and one set of columns. Its 1-entries form a rectangle. Boolean OR combines the rectangles, so overlap on a 1-cell is allowed.
nodes.formula: r_B(A) = min { k : A[x,y] = OR_l (U[x,l] AND V[l,y]) }
assumptions: Factor dimension k may be zero
The empty disjunction is defined as 0

nodes.label: 1-support rectangle cover
nodes.summary: Cover every 1-cell of a binary matrix by all-one row-by-column blocks.
nodes.explanation: A rectangle S x T selects some rows and some columns. It is usable only when every selected cell is 1. A cover reaches every 1-cell; rectangles may overlap. The subscript in rc_1 names the cell value being covered, not a one-witness restriction.
nodes.formula: rc_1(A) = minimum number of all-one rectangles covering supp_1(A)
assumptions: X and Y are finite and nonempty

nodes.label: Fixed-side biclique cover
nodes.summary: Cover a bipartite graph's edges by complete bipartite subgraphs that respect its fixed labeled sides.
nodes.explanation: Keep the disjoint sides X and Y fixed. A biclique with sides S subset X and T subset Y contains exactly the edges represented by the rectangle S x T in the X-by-Y biadjacency matrix.
nodes.formula: bc(G) = minimum number of bicliques covering E(G)
assumptions: Fixed labeled nonempty sides X and Y
Use the X-by-Y biadjacency matrix, not the full symmetric adjacency matrix
The empty family covers an edgeless graph

evidence.locator: Introduction, printed p. 2, biclique-cover and biadjacency paragraphs

nodes.label: Nondeterministic communication depth
nodes.summary: Worst-case accepting protocol depth under the precise Karchmer-Newman-Saks-Wigderson convention.
nodes.explanation: One party has x and the other has y. An accepting branch identifies an all-one rectangle containing (x,y). N^1_S2 is Atlas notation for the source's n(f), measured by maximum leaf depth. It is not deterministic communication complexity and gives no privacy or implementation-latency guarantee.
assumptions: Finite nonempty input sets X and Y
The displayed all-zero totalization is an Atlas convention

evidence.locator: Sections 2.2-2.3, printed pp. 4-5; Proposition 3 and proof for nonempty 1-support

nodes.label: Local Boolean rank
nodes.summary: Minimize the largest number of selected rectangles containing any one row or column.
nodes.explanation: This changes the objective from the total number of rectangles to the heaviest row-or-column participation. It does not count how many rectangles overlap on one matrix cell.
nodes.formula: lr_B(A) = min_C max over rows and columns of rectangle incidence in C
assumptions: Incidence is measured per row or column
X and Y are nonempty so the maximum is defined
The empty cover gives load zero on empty support

evidence.locator: Introduction, printed pp. 2-3, local Boolean-rank definition

nodes.label: Local biclique cover number
nodes.summary: Minimize the largest number of selected covering bicliques containing any one vertex.
nodes.explanation: This is a vertex-load objective for a biclique edge cover. It is distinct from the total number of bicliques and from the number of witnesses covering an individual edge.
nodes.formula: lbc(G) = min_C max_v number of bicliques in C containing v
assumptions: Finite simple graph with fixed labeled nonempty bipartition
The empty cover gives every vertex load zero in an edgeless graph

evidence.locator: Introduction, printed pp. 2-3, local biclique-cover definition

edges.source_scope: Javadi, Maleki and Omoomi supports the factor/rectangle correspondence. It does not separately supply the Atlas empty-support normalization.

witness_translation.forward: For each factor index l, take S_l={x:U[x,l]=1} and T_l={y:V[l,y]=1}. Its support S_l x T_l contains no zero of A, and the union covers every 1-cell; omit empty factors.
witness_translation.reverse: For each chosen all-one rectangle S_l x T_l, use the indicator of S_l as a factor column and the indicator of T_l as a factor row. Their Boolean OR-AND product reconstructs A.
witness_translation.result: A factorization with k factors gives a cover with at most k rectangles after empty factors are omitted, while a cover with t rectangles gives a factorization with exactly t factors. The two inequalities make the minima equal.

local_boundary_case.case: A is all-zero on the still nonempty X and Y
local_boundary_case.argument: The empty Boolean product reconstructs zero and the empty family covers empty support; nonnegative objectives make both minima zero.

notation_boundaries: rc_1 names the covered cell value and maps to S2 kappa(A)
It is not S2 kappa_1(A), which restricts each 1-cell to at most one covering rectangle

edges.statement: For a graph with its fixed labeled bipartition, rc_1(A_G)=bc(G).
assumptions: Fixed labeled nonempty sides X and Y
A_G is the X-by-Y biadjacency matrix
edges.source_scope: Javadi, Maleki and Omoomi supports the rectangle/biclique correspondence. The empty-cover normalization is stated separately by the Atlas.

witness_translation.forward: An all-one rectangle S x T gives the biclique with sides S subset X and T subset Y.
witness_translation.reverse: A covering biclique with sides S subset X and T subset Y gives the all-one rectangle S x T in A_G.
witness_translation.result: Matrix cells and graph edges correspond one-to-one, preserving cover cardinality in both directions.

local_boundary_case.case: G is edgeless on the fixed nonempty sides
local_boundary_case.argument: Both empty families cover the empty target set; nonnegative cardinalities make both minima zero.

notation_boundaries: Use the rectangular biadjacency matrix A_G, not the full symmetric adjacency matrix
The bipartition is part of the data and may not be changed during translation

edges.statement: For nonzero f, N^1_S2(f)=ceil(log_2 rc_1(M_f)); with the separately defined Atlas zero case, N^1_S2(f)=ceil(log_2(max(1,rc_1(M_f)))).
assumptions: For the cited formula, f has at least one 1-input
edges.source_scope: Karchmer, Newman, Saks and Wigderson Proposition 3 and its proof support the nonempty-1-support formula after the explicit notation mapping. The printed logarithm does not resolve rc_1=0.

witness_translation.forward: Given t>=1 covering rectangles, the first party nondeterministically names a row-compatible rectangle using ceil(log_2 t) bits and the second party checks column membership.
witness_translation.reverse: Accepting leaves of a depth-h binary protocol are all-one rectangles covering every 1-input; there are at most 2^h leaves.
witness_translation.result: The two inequalities give the ceiling-log equality for nonempty 1-support under the S2 protocol convention.

adopted_conventions: Set rc_1(M_f)=0 using the empty cover
Use a depth-zero constant-reject protocol and set N^1_S2(f)=0
local_boundary_case.argument: There are no 1-inputs to accept, so constant rejection is sound and complete; depths are nonnegative.

notation_boundaries: N^1_S2 is Atlas notation for S2 n(f)
It is not S2 n_1(f), which restricts witness multiplicity
rc_1 is S2 unrestricted kappa, not kappa_1
This is not deterministic communication complexity
N^0_S2(f):=N^1_S2(1-f) is an Atlas complement-side definition if later displayed

evidence.locator: Sections 2.1-2.3, printed pp. 3-5; Proposition 3 and proof

edges.statement: For a graph with its fixed labeled bipartition, lr_B(A_G)=lbc(G).

Graph objective is maximum biclique incidence per vertex
Neither objective is per-cell or per-edge witness multiplicity

witness_translation.forward: Translate every selected rectangle S x T to the corresponding fixed-side biclique. A row or column belongs to exactly the bicliques containing its corresponding graph vertex.
witness_translation.reverse: Translate each selected fixed-side biclique back to its all-one rectangle; every vertex incidence becomes the corresponding row or column incidence.
witness_translation.result: Every cover retains the same maximum incidence objective, so the minima agree.

local_boundary_case.case: A_G has empty support and G is edgeless on nonempty X and Y

It is not the number of rectangles covering an individual 1-cell and is not S2 bounded witness multiplicity

journeys.title: From a network to a surprising probability
journeys.description: Start with vertices and edges, then follow the circuit interpretation into spanning trees.

steps.prompt: What are the vertices and edges in a triangle?
Give each connection the same conductance.
See how the network becomes a matrix.
Imagine one unit of current entering and leaving.
Measure the voltage needed.

journeys.title: From circuit physics to graph algorithms
journeys.description: Follow the quantity that helps decide which edges to sample.

steps.prompt: How does the rest of the network affect an edge's resistance?
Multiply by conductance to obtain the edge score.
Turn these scores into sampling probabilities.
Specify the property and error that must be preserved.
Read the construction's assumptions before transferring it to a task.

journeys.title: From random walks to an image method
journeys.description: Understand how seeded probabilities connect to a boundary-value problem.

steps.prompt: Imagine moving between neighbouring pixels.
Which labelled seed will be reached first?
Why does each interior probability average neighbouring values?
Treat the seed values as fixed boundary conditions.
Inspect what the model needs and what it does not guarantee.

journeys.title: When adding connections changes a random walk
journeys.description: Follow a random-walk statistic into an electrical calculation, then examine how groups of added edges can interact.

steps.prompt: At each step, choose one neighbour uniformly.
Count the expected steps to reach a destination.
Average over destinations using degree weights, with zero time to the starting vertex.
Use the electrical formula to compute that same average exactly.
Compare individual edge additions with their joint effect. Check the model assumptions before interpreting a larger value.

journeys.title: From a yes/no table to a communication certificate
journeys.description: Follow the same collection of yes-pairs through rectangles, Boolean factors, fixed-side bicliques and one precise nondeterministic communication model.

steps.prompt: Start with a public yes/no table f(x,y). Which labeled pairs are accepted?
Group accepted pairs into row-by-column blocks that contain no rejected pair.
Read each block as one Boolean factor; overlap on accepted cells is allowed.
Keep X and Y fixed and read the same blocks as complete bipartite subgraphs.

If one machine knows x and another knows y, how many bits of branch depth identify a compatible block under the S2 model? Check the all-zero convention and what this does not say about deterministic cost, privacy, latency or deployed systems.

journeys.title: From total cover size to participant load
journeys.description: Compare minimizing the number of covering objects with minimizing how many objects touch any one row, column or vertex.

steps.prompt: First count the total number of rectangles.
Now change the objective to the busiest row or column, not the busiest cell.
Translate that row-or-column load to vertex participation while keeping the bipartition fixed.

opportunities.title: Extend the exact lab to weighted graphs
opportunities.description: Add positive rational conductances while preserving exact arithmetic. The broader theorem is known; the current engine covers unit weights.
acceptance: State the weighted random-walk convention and commute factor.
Compare weighted tree-product enumeration with wₑRₑ.
Reject zero, negative and ambiguous edge weights.

opportunities.title: Formalize a finite bridge in Lean
opportunities.description: Connect a precise graph/circuit statement to a machine-checked proof. This is a formalization task for established mathematics.
acceptance: Locate existing mathlib definitions and record the pinned version.
State all hypotheses and prove the result without placeholders.
Run an independent proof and statement review.

opportunities.title: Ground a connection to a biological model
opportunities.description: Find a primary biological-model paper that uses a compatible graph operator, and state what its modelling assumptions permit.
acceptance: Provide the primary source and exact supporting section.
Specify what vertices, weights and boundary values mean.
Keep model equivalence separate from biological validity.

opportunities.title: Add an explanation a beginner can test
opportunities.description: Explain one existing connection through a small graph and a checkable calculation.
acceptance: Use an in-scope example with a reproducible exact result.
Explain symbols and assumptions in plain language.
Have another reader reproduce it and suggest corrections.

opportunities.title: Find where a proposed transfer breaks
opportunities.description: Construct a small example showing why a stated hypothesis matters. A failed transfer can be a useful contribution.
acceptance: Retain the input and an independent calculation.
Describe the limited conclusion without declaring an entire field unsolved.

opportunities.title: Choose the network measure that fits the application
opportunities.description: Does a random walk with degree-weighted destinations represent the application you care about? Adding edges changes both the walk and those destination weights, so a mathematical increase in K needs interpretation before it supports a practical decision.
acceptance: State the transition rule and how destinations are chosen.
Explain whether destination weights should change when edges are added.
State what an increase in the chosen statistic would mean for the application, and what it would not establish.
opportunities.status: Modelling task; not an asserted open theorem
